subsubtopic: SCALE RESPECTING FEES PAID TO LAWYERS EMPLOYED BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Is any fee scale maintained by the government in regard to fees paid to lawyers doing government legal work and, if so, what are the various items and amounts of this tariff or scale?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: SCALE RESPECTING FEES PAID TO LAWYERS EMPLOYED BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Given the diverse range of legal services performed by lawyers retained to act on behalf of the government, tariffs or scales of fees are maintained only in relation to those services where the activities are routine or the proceedings reasonably well defined. In matters pertaining to the criminal law there is a scale of fees, paid to lawyers retained as agents of the Minister of Justice, the amounts of which vary according to the experience of counsel retained and with the complexity of the professional services being rendered. The range of the tariff is from $20 per hour for preparation and $200 per day in court to $40 per hour for preparation and $400 per day in court. In exceptional cases, $50 per hour for preparation and $500 per day in court may be allowed. In property conveyancing matters, standard services are normally remunerated at a fixed tariff, for example $15 for drafting a standard lease, $50 for a title search under a land registry act, and other services at $20 per hour. In all other non-litigation matters, the fee to be paid to an agent of the Minister of Justice is governed by the level of experience of the lawyer retained, the complexity of the matter in question and, where relevant, the amount of money involved in the case. The fee is normally billed on an hourly basis. In so far as civil litigation is concerned, there is no payment to lawyers, retained as agents of the Minister of Justice, according to a scale or tariff of fees. Agents are expected to charge the same fees that they would ordinarily charge their other clients for similar work, and they are expected to submit an account prepared on an hourly basis.

subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT
speechtext: What is the rationale for requiring contributions to the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act after an employee has accumulated 35 years pensionable contributions when such contributions cease, to the Public Service Superannuation Account after 35 years pensionable service?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT
speechtext: The Advisory Committee, whose recommendations to the President of the Treasury Board were accepted by the government, in proposing the legislation on the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act for submission to parliament in 1970, felt that every employee who was going to benefit under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act should contribute for the valuable new benefits provided under that act so long as that person was employed on a full time basis. There is no relationship between the method of financing the benefits payable from the Superannuation Account under the Public Service Superannuation Act and the method of financing the benefits payable from the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Account under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. Accordingly, in looking for new sources of funds for the payment of benefits under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act there was no reason to limit the period over which contributions should be made.

VETERANS LAND ACT-ELIGIBILITY OF MALE AND FEMALE VETERANS
speechtext:
1.	Under the Veterans Land Act, is any distinction made between a male and a female veteran as to qualifications to acquire loans and, if not, and it can be deduced that a war veteran, whether male or female, can qualify (a) can either the male or female qualify (b) can they both qualify and acquire separate loans and, if not (i) what is the definition of a veteran (ii) what is the regulation that prevents both female and male veteran from qualification, if they are married to one another?
2.	If the regulation states that they both cannot qualify, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
maintopic: VETERANS LAND ACT-ELIGIBILITY OF MALE AND FEMALE VETERANS
speechtext:
1. There is no distinction made between a male and a female veteran as to qualifications to receive a loan, (a) Yes. (b) Section 14 of the Veterans' Land Act Regulations provides that where a husband and wife are both eligible to participate in the benefits of the Veterans' Land Act and a certificate of qualification was issued to each of them, only one such certificate shall be in effect at any one time except where evidence of legal separation has been submitted and the Director is satisfied that the legal separation is not the result of collusion or an understanding between the veteran and his spouse with a view to obtaining any benefits under the act.
2. This regulation reflects the basic principle on which the benefits of the Veterans' Land Act were developed, i.e., that the successful rehabilitation of a veteran on the land was dependent on providing him or her with a built-in equity of up to $2320, non-repayable if the veteran complies for a period of 10 years with the provisions of the VLA purchase contract including residence in the case of a veteran settled as a small holder. The act envisaged the establishment of a veteran and spouse as a family entity because normal matrimonial circumstances precluded any reasonable basis on which separate properties could be purchased for each of them, if they were both eligible and qualified veterans, as they could not be expected to
January 9, 1974

comply with the residence requirement on the separate properties. Re-establishment credit benefits and VLA benefits were alternative one to the other. Where a husband and wife were both veterans and a qualification certificate was issued to each of them, the decision was left to them as to which would apply for the VLA loan. Usually the one who did so was the one who had the smaller re-establishment credit benefit.

maintopic: PERSONAL LOANS MADE BY CHARTERED BANKS
PERSONAL LOANS MADE BY CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
1.	What rules have been established for chartered banks regarding the way personal loans are to be made?
2.	Can the chartered banks loan up to 100 per cent of deposits on hand?
3.	Do the same rules apply in the case of loans made to firms?
4.	What percentage of the deposits must chartered banks deposit with the Bank of Canada as reserves?

maintopic: PERSONAL LOANS MADE BY CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
1 and 3. The
general powers of banks to make loans with or without security, including personal and business loans, are set out in Section 75 of the Bank Act. Banks are prohibited under Section 138 of the Act from making an agreement with another bank with respect to the rate of interest or charges on a loan. Under Section 92 of the Act and the Bank Cost of Borrowing Disclosure Regulations of September 27, 1967, banks are required to disclose the cost of borrowing on personal loans. Subject to such provisions, a chartered bank is permitted in competition with other banks and other financial institutions to establish its own rules regarding the way personal and business loans are to be made.
2. The relationship of the total outstanding loans of a bank to its total deposits is not laid down in the Bank Act and varies depending on the policy and operations of each bank. The statement of assets and liabilities of the chartered banks, published each month in the Canada Gazette, indicates that at October 31, 1973, the total outstanding loans of all chartered banks were approximately 59% of total deposits.
4.	Under Section 72 of the Bank Act, a bank must maintain a minimum cash reserve in the form of notes of, and deposits in Canadian currency with, the Bank of Canada, such reserve not to be less on the average during any month than an amount equal to 12% of its deposit liabilities payable on demand in Canadian currency and 4% of its deposit liabilities as are payable after notice in Canadian currency. Each bank must maintain a secondary reserve, in addition to its cash reserve, comprised of treasury bills and day to day loans to investment dealers plus any cash reserves that are in excess of the minimum requirement, such reserve not to be less on the average during any month than 8% currently of its deposit liabilities as are payable in Canadian currency.

speechtext:
Motion No. 1.
That Bill C-236, An Act to provide a means to conserve the supplies of petroleum products within Canada during periods of national emergency caused by shortages or market disturbances affecting the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada, and to amend the National Energy Board Act, be amended in Sub-clause 2(1) thereof by deleting the words "or any province" in lines 28 and 29 on page 2.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill, like the child who goes to kindergarten, comes back from committee in a much better state than it was in when it left this House. It is less repugnant to us now than it was before but there are still a number of areas where, in our opinion, it can be greatly improved. I think the bill is going to pass anyway. During the course of discussion on the amendments we will have some comments to make which we think may be of some use, and hopefully some of our amendments will be accepted.
January 9, 1974

I have said that the bill will pass. This is obvious when you see how deeply and passionately those two parties favour the bill. The government favours it. Of course, the government position is always to take more power whenever it can, without any action. The government's position on this is like that of the usual bureaucrat when approaching a problem-when in doubt, mumble; when in charge, ponder; and when in trouble, delegate. That is just what the government is doing with this legislation. We have had enough promises, enough talks, enough declarations, enough statements made by members of the cabinet over the last few years which, if stretched end to end, would reach from Victoria to Halifax and would provide enough material to fuel this building for several years. But, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to action, to things to be done, to be anticipated in expectation of this problem, there has been nothing at all. If actions were clothes to cover nakedness or naked policies, then the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) in my opinion would tie for the title "Mr. Nude Canada of 1973".
With respect to the members of the party to my left and the approach which they took in committee, and which they will probably repeat in the House, they also love to see large, undiluted quantities of power given-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but it is extremely difficult for the Chair to hear him. May we have order, please. It is extremely difficult for the Chair, and hon. members interested in the debate, to follow the hon. member who has the floor if all the conversations that are taking place in the chamber continue as at present.

The hon. members should recognize that the floor was given to one of their colleagues, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). If some members want to talk, they should go behind the curtains or in the lobby.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. If the conversations continued it would mean that any faint hope I might have of converting hon. members opposite, or hon. members to my left, would be lost. My only hope is if they hear me, understand me and believe me. I was dealing with the approach to be taken by hon. members to my left to this particular amending motion, and to the bill generally. I have not much hope that their attitude will change. We have observed their very subservient and obsequious attitude toward the government on this subject. It is a sad situation. As I sit and observe them I say, speaking in the kindest possible way and not in any political sense, that the present front bench of the socialist party can be compared to a group of withered Buddhas presiding over the ruins of party purity.
It is quite true, Mr. Speaker, that some patently phony issues were raised by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) yesterday, and I will deal with them when we come to the appropriate amendment. I simply use this occasion to point out that it is the view of this party, and the view which fortunately the government was persuad-
Energy Supplies Emergency Act ed to accept, that any declaration as to a national emergency must be approved by parliament; that any situation which would come about if the position suggested by the hon. member for York South were accepted, would mean that there could be a declaration by this House following an order by the cabinet as to a national emergency; and that a declaration by this House, and the debate which would follow, that no national emergency existed could be circumvented and vetoed by the other place. That is something which this party will not tolerate.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext: It is the other way around.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The hon. member will have a chance to express his view, but he has put himself and his party in an odious position which indicates that he has no faith in the virtue of this House to deal with and set aside an order made by the government if the facts do not justify it. That is what this party wants; it is what this party has always sought and we now have it in reasonable form. I compliment the minister for his astuteness, after some considerable persuasion, in accepting this particular proposition.
I shall not detain the House very long with regard to this amendment, but I think it is essential that we go into it. It gives us an opportunity to find out at the very beginning, in the definition clause, what is involved in this bill, what it could lead to and what the probable consequences are as well as how they may affect other jurisdictions in the country. The amendment is very simply to delete the words "or any province" from the interpretation of the words "wholesale customer" which appear in clause 2, the interpretation clause.
I do not think it will do any harm from the viewpoint of continuity to put the present definition on the record so that it will appear in the context of my remarks. As the bill now reads, "wholesale customer" is defined as:
. .. any person who purchases any controlled product in bulk at the wholesale level and includes Her Majesty in right of Canada or any province, any agent thereof-
Then, it goes on to deal with other groups, other institutions and other classes. My amendment is for the purpose of deleting the words "or any province". I know it is true to say that to some extent-and I am probably anticipating the minister in this-the provinces are substantial users of petroleum products. But in the words of my leader, while they are not sovereign powers in their own right, they have, within the limits of their responsibility, what are in effect sovereign powers as well as some very important functions with respect to the people who have elected the governments of those provinces.
May I point out what some of the functions of a provincial authority are? They are, the construction and maintaining of roads; the use of buildings, which obviously includes the extent to which certain buildings will be used and the fuel to be used to heat them; the providing of fuel for utilities, and I am thinking in particular of those provinces which maintain their own utility corporations as a public service-Manitoba, British Columbia and Ontario are typical examples. Those provinces and their people have seen fit to establish public corporations for the provision of electric power, among other utility powers, to the people of the province. This is something

January 9, 1974
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
which has to be taken into account when we consider whether the word "province" should be included in this definition of "wholesale customer". There are other provinces which maintain, have maintained, and no doubt will continue to maintain certain facilities for providing transportation for the people. I could go on but I shall limit the list for the purpose of my argument.
What could happen is that any of the provincial governments with regard to maintaining and continuing the services of this kind will, if this bill goes through in its present form, if an emergency is declared and approved by parliament and if a mandatory allocation program is established, have to come hat in hand to a five member board in Ottawa to seek permission for the use of fuel to be supplied by suppliers, as defined, to the provinces as wholesale customers. That is the situation which concerns me.
I recognize that there is another aspect which is covered: British Columbia, for example, has established a marketing board which will take possession of or market certain fuels which are made available in the province. As this bill now stands, under the definitions which I have given to the House and under the right of the Energy Supplies Allocation Board to establish prices, it would then be competent for this five member board to say to the province of British Columbia, "You cannot supply fuel which has come into the legal ownership of your marketing board to any of your own provincial agencies within British Columbia; under no circumstances can you do that unless we give you a certain permit to indicate type, amount, quantity, date and so on." Those are problems which have to be faced.
I want to make another point, Mr. Speaker. The minister knows, as do I and a lot of other people, the very doubtful constitutional character of this legislation. Let us be clear: this body has not and never will take the position, if circumstances warrant the declaration of an emergency, that there should be any constitutional challenge so far as we are concerned. But we are not able to answer for other people in Canada; we are not able to answer for provincial authorities in Canada. We will get a chance to go into this later, but the minister knows that under the jurisprudence which now prevails, the question of an emergency is not a question for the government. It is not even a question for this parliament.
The existence of an emergency which justifies a federal government taking powers and authority to deal with matters such as contractual relationships, and natural resources lying entirely within the control of a province, is a matter of fact. The courts have held this. The Supreme Court of Canada and the Privy Council, in the days when the Privy Council still had jurisdiction, have held this. That position is supported by the litigation which was dealt with after the first world war and the second world war. The question of whether there is an emergency is a matter of fact and if it does exist, the government can legislate. The courts have held that if the federal government legislates in accordance with the terms of that emergency, it has the right to overrule provincial rights and provincial jurisdiction. That is as it should be. We do not challenge that right.

Let me suggest the doubtful legal basis on which this bill stands in its present wording. Theoretically-I admit that this is most unlikely to happen-if the Prime Minister were to wake up one morning and find that the fuel for heating his house had been shut off, he could have the cabinet declare a national emergency and then ask this House to support it. The bill, conceivably, could provide for that. Fortunately, we have been able to persuade the government to allow its decision in that regard to be debated in Parliament.
I am concerned about the position of the provinces. I do not suppose, unless members on the government side change their position or unless I am more persuasive than I have been in the past, that this amendment will pass. Yet we are responsible, on behalf of the people of Canada, for seeing that the best possible bill is passed and that the legislation, in its final form, has as few imperfections in it as possible. Therefore it is my duty to speak of the dangers of including provisions of the kind I have mentioned.
I do not know if any province would see fit to challenge the government declaration. I hope not. If the circumstances warrant the government's declaring an emergency, no one would challenge that. Yet I want to emphasize again the doubtful legal foundation on which this legislation rests and indicate that, beyond any shadow of a doubt, there are real dangers in this. I hope that the exclusion of the relevant words might remove those dangers.
I have looked through the bill and have spoken of the powers contained in it. The regulatory provisions give the board to be established power to establish pricing systems. The government through the board, may make regulations with regard to wholesale customers. It can establish pricing systems which are binding upon provincial authorities which become owners of petroleum products, natural gas or coal, or the products of those fuels which are to be allocated by an order. This board can say to provincial authorities, "We will tell you how much you can charge your own provincial organizations, your own provincial services and facilities, for the fuel which is produced in your province and which belongs to the government and people of that province." I am not arguing about the powers of provincial authorities vis-a-vis the federal authority. I am merely pointing out some dangers that my party, in moving certain amendments, wishes to avoid.
This five-man board can demand from any provincial authorities information with regard to present and past accounts. It can ask for information as to pricing, as to forecasts, projections, and so on. One only needs to read the regulatory section to note the vast powers, quantitatively and qualitatively, with which this board will be invested. I, therefore, say that in dealing with this bill, the House should proceed with the utmost caution and examine and survey each particular issue raised in it.
I do not know how much fuel in the provinces might be involved in any allocation order or how much fuel, which would be subject to an allocation order by the board, the provinces have been using for themselves. We attempted to look into these things in committee but were met by what will be known in future as the "Macdonald principle" underlying the calling and examining of witnesses.
January 9, 1974

We were told at that time that government witnesses, departmental witnesses, witnesses from the National Energy Board or administration officials, and the minister can correct me if I am paraphrasing him wrongly, could only appear with the permission of the minister, could only say what the minister allowed them to say and that, in the final analysis, it was competent for the minister to control these witnesses appearing before the standing committee. That is a pernicious doctrine which, some day, I hope will be challenged.
If that doctrine prevails, what will it do to the Public Accounts Committee, or to all standing committees? It is essential that members of parliament should be able to come to a committee and obtain information on which to base their attitude towards any legislative proposal. We learned of the attitude of the minister, and that the government wanted this legislation put through with great haste. We do not disagree with the need to legislate with reasonable promptitude. On the other hand, we want reasonable opportunity to make careful and reasonable scrutiny of the provisions of this bill. Hon. members were sent to this House for the purpose of ascertaining such things. Of that opportunity we were deprived.

The real question of substance involved in this amendment is whether the government of Canada was unreasonably interfering with the powers of provincial governments in this regard. I suppose the best evidence as to whether there has been any neglect to act reasonably would come from the provincial governments themselves.
I can say to the hon. gentleman and to the House that, while comments on the bill have been received from various provincial governments which will be most affected by it-and, indeed, we have sought their view on the proposal both before it was submitted to the House and subsequently-there has been no objection as far as I am aware to the particular clause which the hon. member now seeks to amend. I think it was well understood at the meeting of energy ministers on November 23 that if facts do materialize of such a nature as to bring about a national emergency it would not only be appropriate, from the standpoint of the provinces, but an obligation on the part of the Government of Canada to assume the emergency powers embodied in the act in order to make certain that the wider interest of the public should be protected.
The position which I took in committee, and which I take again today is, therefore, to ask the House not to accept this particular amendment. To do so would mean that an allocation intended to provide for certain individuals within the community, either because of their special circumstances or because of their priority need, would be subject to the individual judgments of provincial agencies which, as the hon. member for Peace River has said, already possess extensive jurisdiction in this regard. It is not unfair to comment that, from time to time during the course of this particular crisis of supply in the entire western world, some provincial governments have been inclined to look upon their obligations to supply users in other provinces in a very narrow sense and have been inclined to object to the suggestion that there should be any extensive application of this provision through eastern Canada. I, therefore, think it is reasonable that one agency should be responsible for looking after the over-all needs of Canadians affected by the bill and ultimately deciding on the priorities.
Further with regard to the interests of the provinces, the hon. gentleman has raised the question whether this agency under federal authority will take account of provincial claims. I would remind the House, as I said in committee and at the second reading stage, that when we described this proposal in general terms to the provincial ministers of energy on November 23, they specifically asked that not one but two provinces be represented on the committee. We accepted that proposition, which meant raising the number of board members to five, with the stipulation that one appointment was to be made from among nominees suggested by a producing province, in this case Alberta, and another from those suggested by a consuming province, Quebec. I look forward to receiving from the Province of Alberta the name of the nominee

suggested. We have already received suggestions from Quebec. In other words, the board will be representative of the experience possessed by the National Energy Board, of the experience accumulated at provincial level from the standpoint of a producing province and of the interest of the consuming public in a more general sense.
In summary, then, it seems to me to be in the interest of the nation generally that the board, acting under these emergency powers, should have the ability to protect all Canadians and that this ability should not be curtailed by prior claims made, perhaps, out of an excess of zeal, by individual provincial civil servants. It should not be curtailed by the claims of provincial agencies but the needs of all Canadians should be taken into account. This tribunal which, after all, would include representatives nominated by the provinces, should be able to determine the priority given to allocations in the event of any shortages. On this basis I invite the House to reject the hon. gentleman's amendment.

speechtext:
Motion No. 2.
That Bill C-236, an Act to provide a means to conserve the supplies of petroleum products within Canada during periods of national emergency caused by shortages or market disturbances affecting the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada, and to amend the National Energy Board Act, be amended in Sub-clause 9(4) thereof by deleting the words "or purported exercise" in line 19 on page 5.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is another amendment for the purpose of deleting three words. Unless anyone here may say this is simply a matter of semantics, I wish to assert the contrary. We are dealing in this legislation with a board which would have greater power in peacetime than was, quite possibly, delegated even in wartime to any similar group since the days of Ghengis Khan-perhaps I shall be able to find a more modern analogy later on.
My colleagues and I have already enumerated the vast powers being given to this board, powers which could be used to ride roughshod over the rights of everyone from provincial governments to individual consumers. Clause 9 deals with the authority of the board and the power of the board to delegate-in itself significant.
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
Finally, in subclause (4), the offensive subclause, the board and its members are exempt from liability in respect of any act or thing done or purported to be done in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of a duty or power under the act. Mr. Speaker, if these words were subject to the amendment I am moving, if the words to which I am objecting were excluded, I would find no objection to the subclause. I think it is proper that a board of this nature should be given a measure of immunity. If the board or one of its members does something in the course of exercising the functions or powers prescribed in the act, and does it in good faith, I think they should be protected from the possibility of civil or criminal proceedings being taken.
But bearing in mind the substantial powers with which the board is vested-and I urge all hon. members to read the bill carefully to find out how extensive these powers really are-I suggest that a clause which purports to allow a member of the board to act outside the powers parliament is being asked to confer and still enjoy full immunity is altogether unacceptable. One could follow the trails left by the injuries, losses and damages sustained by thousands and thousands of people affected by the rules and regulations of similar boards which were established during the first and second world wars. One could follow the proceedings of, and read the evidence given to, boards that were established to find out how much damage was in fact inflicted on the one side, and suffered on the other side, by people or institutions who had to comply with the orders of those boards.
I suggest to the members of this House that it would be entirely unwarranted to give this board an invitation- because that is what the clause amounts to-to go forth as the good and faithful servant of the government and to do something that is quite outside the scope of the act and outside the scope of its duties. Then, all you would have to do would be to say that you acted in good faith and you would be free from any sanction. I cannot buy that.
I am quite willing that the board operate within the four corners of this piece of legislation. If it makes an error of judgment, it then has protection. But to allow the board or its members, or possibly even people who receive a delegation of authority under the first part of the clause, to handle a matter in their own way, entirely ignoring the act and the regulations, or its mandatory allocation program, perhaps in some cases causing irremedial damage to certain people, and then to be freed from any form of punitive action or sanction simply because they said they acted in good faith, we simply cannot accept. After all, acting in good faith can mean a lot of things. In a clause of this sort, all it means is that they can say they thought it was a good thing for the country to do what they did, and that would free them from punitive action. I would object to those powers being given to a board that has only the usual powers and authority.
It is a sad commentary on the kind of world we live in, when crises, or alleged crises, or rumours of crises abound, that we all flock forward and give this kind of power to the government. It is a shocking, shameful thing, and is one of the reasons, to a great extent, that civilized countries today find themselves sometimes incapable of han-

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the argument of my learned friend in his discussion of this "purported" amendment, but I must confess that I do not agree with him. It seems to me that, as it stands now, this clause affords a necessary and reasonable protection to anyone who assumes the very important responsibilities of this board.
I would remind the House that the words are "in good faith". If anyone acts in a way that is not in good faith, then they can be made responsible for what they do. But if they do act in good faith, they should not be harassed by the possibility of legal proceedings being brought against them, perhaps because they made some mistake in the exercise of their powers, or perhaps because a court declared that they should not have done what they did or that they did not have the legal authority for doing what they did. I say that if they nevertheless act in good faith, they deserve to be protected.
I doubt very much whether any person of the calibre required for this particular job would be very happy about accepting his responsibilities if he knew that he would be liable to legal harassment if he made a mistake, which in my view would be the result of this proposed, purported amendment. This language is not unfamiliar to those

versed in legal matters. Other people, such as magistrates, sometimes perform functions of lesser importance than the members of this board will be required to perform, but they are protected so long as they act in good faith in the carrying out of their duties. From our point of view this amendment is unnecessary, and indeed might be harmful to the carrying out of the purposes of the act.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member would answer this question. I tried to follow him closely, and I always respect his legal abilities. He emphasized that the words are "in good faith". Would he tell the House what is the difference between the words "in good faith in the exercise of a duty or power" and the words "in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of a duty or power"?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ALLOCATION BOARD, MANDATORY ALLOCATION OF SUPPLIES AND RATIONING OF CONTROLLED PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is quite a considerable difference, as I understand it. I am a little rusty in my law and my friend may be able to correct me if I give him the wrong interpretation, but my view of the matter is this. The words "in good faith" have to do with the approach, with the mental attitude, of a person. Are you trying to carry out your duty in the way you are required to do so? Are you carrying out your duty without personal malice or personal bias? If so, you would be acting in good faith.
On the other hand, supposing you were to make an order that for some reason was irregular or which the court holds is improper for some legal reason. You would then be not acting in the exercise of a duty or power but in the purported exercise of a duty or power. A person who, in perfectly good faith, makes a mistake in law or a mistake in fact is protected by the words "or purported exercise", whereas he is not protected if those words are struck out. I think the protection should be broad enough to cover anybody who is trying his best to do a job, acting without malice, without improper motives and without bias in seeking to perform his duty, even though he may happen to make some mistake in law or conceivably a mistake in fact which would deprive him of his powers under the act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to make in substance the same point already made by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) whom I recall from the distant past, when I was practising law and he was practising it with more distinction, had something of a reputation as an expert on prerogative writs. During a study of this particular question of excess of powers, I would listen to that hon. member with some attention because he had occasion from time to time to act on the other side on these particular questions.
On the point which he has expressed, I would agree that the question of good faith would be a question of fact under the circumstances of a particular case, and the question as to whether it was an excess in the exercise of powers would really be a question of law depending upon the technical interpretation of this particular statute. As has already been mentioned, the statute is a highly technical one, but one under which it would not be difficult at all, from the standpoint of a legal interpretation, to arrive at a situation where there was an action which legally might be described as an action in excess of the powers.

The basic position I took in the committee, which I will repeat, is that it seems to me apt and just that action should be taken, as it can be taken against the board, under the Federal Courts Act. Under the provisions of that act, a review of the exercise of jurisdiction can be taken by prerogative writ, by declaration or perhaps by injunction. Legal action might be taken against the board in that way, or political action might be taken against the ministry which, after all, remains responsible for the board.
It seems to me to be a basic fundamental that individuals who are appointed should not be made personally liable so long as they acted in good faith, and also in the belief they were exercising a power which had been conferred upon them by the statute. It seems to me the appropriate legal method in these circumstances is not one that seeks to put individuals acting on this board into personal bankruptcy. I would remind hon. members that we will be dealing here with not just thousands of dollars but potentially hundreds of thousands of dollars in terms of orders which may have to be made from time to time.
The least useful way, and perhaps I bring bias to this as the son of a former public servant, in this bill or any bill that comes before this parliament, would be to seek to exercise the jurisdiction of the courts against an individual public servant by putting his personal assets up to the possibility of a writ for suit. It is on this basis we opposed the amendment in committee and will oppose it again today.
The hon. member for Peace River made reference to the fact that this power would give the members of the tribunal the right, and I noted his words, to ignore the act, ignore the regulations and to disregard whatever their powers might be; that is a matter of question. I would point out that that would be a matter of good faith in the circumstances, the question of the excess of jurisdiction, which is the point to which the word "purport" refers, is a question of law which would have to be determined by the courts under the circumstances. Therefore, I would hope, for the better exercise of this jurisdiction, that this can be left with the tribunal.
The point has been made, and I reiterate it, but for this protection it would be entirely possible for private interests to seek to harass members of the board by making them personally liable for actions taken not only in good faith but in the genuine belief that they were acting within their powers. Nothing could make the exercise of the important jurisdiction of this board more difficult than the threat of that kind of personal action against a public servant.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask the minister to reconsider his position. I will try to make my point clear without getting into the question of what might happen under the act, as that has already been gone into by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin).
The bill provides;
The Board and its members are exempt from liability for any act or thing done or admitted by the Board in good faith in the exercise or purported exercise of a duty or power under this Act.
That certainly protects the members as far as the minister wants to go. Surely, that protects them if the board
Energy Supplies Emergency Act acts in good faith in the exercise of a duty or power under the act, but when you include the word "purported" I think it is contradictory. I have a dictionary here which gives a brief definition of the word "purport", and I think this is what the hon. member for Peace River was driving at. It suggests that purport in respect of a document or a subject has the meaning of conveying a state or professing to do something, or intending to seem to do it. This definition really makes the situation worse than has been described. I do not think you can purport to exercise a duty or power if you are acting in good faith because that would be totally contradictory. I do not know why this phrase is in there at all, except in the case of the board deciding to deliberately ignore the terms and conditions of the act and the regulations laid down by the Cabinet. As long as they purport to exercise a duty or power under this act they would escape liability.
Surely, all we are trying to do is make certain that the members of this all-powerful board, and it will be powerful when we implement this bill, are exempt from liability when they act in good faith in the exercise of a duty or a power. I agree with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), although he differs in interpretation, that the important words are "in good faith". If you exercise a power in good faith or a duty in good faith, providing you do so to the best of your ability, honestly and without any idea of committing a fraud you should be protected. If you purport to do something, then I suggest this is totally contradictory. In fact, I think this phrase was thrown in by some civil servant who was worried that he might get into some trouble so he put in another word he found in the dictionary to make the protection broader.
The minister suggests that the courts will interpret this, but surely it is a function of this parliament to legislate clearly and precisely in order that there will not be that kind of difficulty in the courts. There has been a great complaint about lawyers not being clear and precise, and I think parliament should make the statutes very clear. We have referred to the phrase "in good faith", but when you suggest that a member purports to do something, or makes out to do it, surely that is contradictory.
It is because of this difficulty that I directed my question to the hon. member for Greenwood. If we want to legislate in this way, I suppose the amendment is not particularly important because, it does not go to the root of the bill, and there has been an agreement by the various parties that the matter of declaring an emergency will, in the final analysis, be referred to parliament. So, there is some protection. I cannot see for the life of me why the minister, who is a lawyer, wants that word "purport" left in, except perhaps because some civil servant put it in there. Like most ministers, once his officials put something in, he will not remove it. You cannot get a minister to remove anything. It seems to me that the members of this board will have all the protection they need, and by leaving out the word "purport" the clause would be better worded and would not be contradictory.

Because of the wording of this bill there is a possibility that, as a result of an allocation, a corporation may suffer a loss. The point of the phrase is a technical one. This is an administrative clause and the phrase is included to protect public servants, that is members of the board, from personal law suits. I suggest it is as simple as that.
If we remove the word "purported", as the Conservatives would have us to do, then I put the question to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) who then would want to serve on the board? Who would take the risk if he knew there was a loophole by which he could be sued personally because of the implementation of this emergency legislation. If we face a real emergency in respect of fuel, we need very capable people on this board. If we were to in any way cast doubt on a person's security in serving on this board we would only weaken the capability of the government to make a decision concerning whether or not an emergency should be declared.
It seems to me the Conservative Party is concerned that we know the facts as to whether or not it is necessary to have a national emergency declared. Therefore, we need capable people on this board, and I cannot see them serving if this risk is involved. Indeed, who on the board would dare make a decision if, having traced down the line of responsibility, he found there could be a possibility of a personal lawsuit against him. I think members of this House will see the necessity to leave this sub-clause as it is and we will reject the Conservative amendment.

Very briefly, Mr. Speaker, I will follow the admonition of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) and remain impartial on this question. I want to say, with respect that this particular clause, that when I looked at it in the first instance I wondered whether in fact there was a need for the words "or purported exercise". The more I studied it the more I became convinced they were, in fact, necessary. Notwithstanding the caveat filed by the hon. member for Peace River, I think we are getting into a debate on legal semantics. It seems to me that under the clause we could have simply indicated that the difference is that if the individual acts pursuant to his authority in the exercise of his duty or power there would be no problem. I think the expression, in good faith, really applies more effectively to the purported exercise of a particular duty or power.
Perhaps I might draw this analogy to illustrate what I mean. An individual, let us say in the Canadian armed forces, has the use of a vehicle from Monday to Friday. In the interest of answering an emergency on a Saturday he uses that particular vehicle. In effect, he is acting in good faith in the purported exercise of his duty. Eventually, someone will have to decide whether he made the right decision and whether, in deciding to use that particular vehicle on the Saturday, he was purporting to exercise his duty. Clearly, he is not exercising but is purporting to

exercise his duty. I think that is the analogy I would use to indicate that there is, in fact, a difference between exercising authority under the jurisdiction given and purporting to do so. So, I think there is a necessity for these three words to be incorporated.

Now, if an emergency were declared, the government would not be standing alone. If its recommendation were passed, the government would have the support of the opposition, or at least a majority of the members of this House of Commons. It seems to me, if I were sitting on the treasury benches, I would feel my hand was strengthened if the representatives of the people of Canada were behind me. I think the prejudice-I can only call it an outburst of prejudice-by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie is unjustified in the circumstances.
As the minister has said, we are dealing with an important bill. We are dealing with an important bill because of the powers it gives the government, sanctioned we hope by Parliament. I would be inclined to agree with the hon. member that the government would have to stand or fall on that judgment under the circumstances. Potentially it could be a dangerous statute. Everything that flows from it as a result of that right could be dangerous.

I do not think I have ever read any statute of Parliament, including the War Measures Act, which is so all-embracing or all encompassing in respect of the way it can gather under an umbrella the resources, the transportation facilities, the production facilities of the country, as related to energy. I will have no objection to a question at the end of my comments. I do not have a copy of the statutes in front of me with regard to the appointment of, let us say, provincial judges, federal court judges or others who exercise certain powers over citizens. However, 1 have read these statutes, and I do not recall seeing in them any provision whereby a person is given protection for acting outside his authority merely, as the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) says, because he professed to be acting within it. To my mind this would seem to be stretching matters just a wee bit. The minister, in defending the position taken by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), used the tactic that is often used when one describes judges. One will say of judges who decide cases in one's favour that they are marvellous, and of course that the others ought never to have been appointed. He embraced the argument of the hon. member for Greenwood. His argument was that this was a highly technical statute, and of course the minister agreed. I contend that it is not a highly technical statute at all. As I read it, it is a gathering of all of the powers to this board in the proper circumstances, supported by a resolution of parliament.
Someone says that they have the protection of the prerogative writs that are in the Federal Court Act. This is supposed to be a quick remedy. Mr. Speaker, it is some time since the minister practised law in the Federal Court of Canada, or in any court. I do not say that in any derogatory sense because he has been involved in the government of this country, but I point out to him that that is not a speedy remedy by any stretch of the imagination. I say this as one not that far distant from the practice of law.
Frankly I am somewhat dismayed that the group to my left, which on occasion in this parliament, in fact recently in this parliament, found themselves on the side of civil libertarians should now suddenly find themselves in a position where they would deny what seems to me to be an ordinary restriction on the power of any board, namely, that providing the board is acting in good faith the officials will have protection. However, if the board does not act in good faith, and officials act outside the limits of the statute, even though they profess to be acting within the statute-self-serving, of course-then they should not be protected.
I think the latter matter raised by one of the other speakers who preceded me related to the question of personal bankruptcy in the event something of this nature occurred. But surely the government of Canada is not in a different position than, let us say, the city of Toronto was on one occasion when a member of its police force acted illegally in carrying out his duties. I am sure he thought he acted legally, and the city of Toronto on that occasion decided to stand behind that person financially.

We think this is a different piece of legislation.
What we are concerned with in this legislation is the fact that an emergency could arise in this country during which Canadians might be suffering extreme cold. Canadians might be freezing. In those circumstances, the government should not only have authority to declare an emergency and act accordingly, but it should be obligated to take such steps. We do not share the view of some of my friends to the right on the proposition that the right of the government in these circumstances should be shackled. We are a bit afraid that if the right to declare an emergency and to deal with it is burdened with the necessity of calling parliament when parliament is not here, the government could err in not declaring an emergency when it ought to do so.
However, it sounds like a good idea that if there has been an order in council declaring an emergency, it ought to come before parliament. In spite of what I just said about the difference between this kind of emergency and emergencies involving infringements of civil liberties, we are prepared to go along with the main purport of this amendment which is that an order in council establishing an emergency having been passed, within a certain period of time that order must be approved by this House of Commons.
I must point out, however, that we take the strongest possible exception to the idea that it must also be approved by the other place or, in other words, that the following type of situation could develop. There could be shortages of energy and fuel in this country to the point where Canadian were suffering. The government could take the view that there was an emergency, and could express it in an order in council. This House of Commons, which contains the elected members of the people of Canada, could take the same view and say yes, there is an emergency, and we approve of what the government has done. Yet their Honours in the other place could veto the decision of the government and the decision of this House of Commons. I submit that is a shameful thing for the government to be placing before us at this time.
Energy Supplies Emergency Act
When I was referring to the place of the Senate a while ago, I overheard one of my friends to the right use the word "parliament". I suppose that was an attempt to remind me that parliament consists of more than the House of Commons, and that there is a constitutional obligation for everything that is decided to be decided by both Houses. May I remind the hon. member that parliament consists of three entities and not just two. It consists of the Senate, the House of Commons and the representative of the Crown. If you talk about having a resolution approved by both Houses, you are still not having it approved by parliament as a whole. It is only when you bring in a bill, have it passed by both Houses and submitted for Royal Assent that it becomes an act of parliament in its entirety.
I remind the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), who has been following me with interest, that there are instances when decisions under legislation are made by this House of Commons and by this House of Commons alone. I ask my hon. friend to look at Section 91(1) of the British North America Act which, among other things, provides that there shall be no tampering with the provision that a parliament must not last longer than five years. In that same Section 91(1), approved by this House of Commons and the other place, there are words that say that that provision can be set aside, that in time of war or emergency, real or apprehended, the length of a parliament can be extended, provided it is not opposed by more than one third of the members of the House of Commons.
What decision could be more serious to our democratic way of life than the right to extend, even in wartime, the life of parliament and yet in our sacred document, the constitution, it is clearly spelled out that the decision on that matter is made solely and exclusively by the House of Commons. Do not tell me that I am ignoring parliament as a whole or suggesting something new or unique when I say there are times when decisions are made by the House of Commons alone, and there are times when it ought to be that way. I did not have the time nor the research assistance that some people have to do all the searching of records and documents that I wanted to do. I went on the assumption this might not come up until tomorrow or the next day. However, I do know from my memory of some other instances.
For example, in the Government Organization Act of 1970, there is provision for the government to establish additional ministries of state, or ministers of state, or both. That act provides that if the government passes an order in council establishing a new ministry of state, it cannot come into effect until that order in council has been tabled in this House of Commons and approved by this House of Commons, but only by this House of Commons. Incidentally, that was put in there largely at the instigation and urging of my friends in the Progressive Conservative Party. In 1970, they were quite satisfied that the establishment of an additional ministry could be put into effect if it had a favourable decision by this House of Commons and by this House of Commons alone.
In looking at a situation in which people might be freezing because of shortages of energy or fuel, why must we give a veto to the other place? Members know what

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if I were to ask hon. members what is the most serious action taken by the executive since the end of the second world war, in nine cases out of ten, if not in 99 cases out of 100, I would get the same answer,-that the most serious executive act on the part of the government was the declaration of the War Measures Act in peacetime in October 1970. As a matter of fact, the government was not obliged to submit a motion even to the House of Commons. It was an act of democracy on the part of the government of which we approved. Paul Martin tabled in that House the Order in Council invoking the War Measures Act together with related correspondence. But there was no debate on the matter in the other House. If it is part of our history that the most serious executive action most people can remember was made subject to the approval of the House of Commons alone, it is utterly preposterous for the government to say that if an emergency is declared because people are freezing and need power the question should be submitted not only for the approval of the House of Commons but for the approval of the business people, the magnates, the directors and so on, in the other place. It is completely wrong, and I urge the government as strongly as I can to agree to the amendment I am about to propose.
We do not object to the idea that the government should bring the matter before parliament. On balance, we say there is merit in it. We have become involved in a lot of gobbledygook in this clause because of the need to anticipate three kinds of situations, first, a declaration being made when the House is sitting, second, when the House is in recess, and, third, when the House is away during a period of prorogation. I am not saying there is anything wrong with it. I am accepting it. I am commenting on it. I shall take only a few minutes more. I thank the House for its courtesy. I hope anyone speaking to this amendment will explain why it is so much more important to bring the Senate into this than it was to bring the Senate into the declaration of the War Measures Act. After all, we are dealing here with something which affects plain, ordinary Canadians who may be cold. We are their elected representatives and we should determine whether the government should proceed with the proposition it makes that there is an emergency.
Now, to achieve this change, this denial of the right of veto to the Senate, I am going to move an amendment to motion No. 4. As I started to say a moment ago before I was interrupted, motion No. 4 has a lot of language in it and it would be extremely difficult to draft an amendment to cut the Senate out in all the places that it appears in the motion. Therefore, I am not going to interfere at all with the obligation that the order be tabled in the other place as well as here. I am not going to interfere with the right of the other place to debate it, or with the regulations that apply to that debate, or even with their right to vote on it. But I am going to insist that this House should not give the Senate, by their vote, the right of veto. How they vote simply should not count.
My proposal is simply that we change subclause (9) in the proposed motion. That subclause now states:
If either House of Parliament negatives the motion that an order made under subsection (1) be concurred in, the order is thereupon revoked.
I propose we change that wording to read as follows:
If the House of Commons negatives the motion that an order made under subsection (1) be concurred in, the order is thereupon revoked.
I have this in proper amendment form and I shall read it in just a moment, but may I make clear what it would do. If my amendment carries-and I plead with this House in the name of democracy and in the name of the rights of the ordinary people of this country to accept my amendment-what would happen is that if there is an emergency, then parliament is either sitting or is called, the order is laid on the table in both Houses, debates take place, but it is the vote in this House that prevails. If the order place votes the same way as this House, that is fine. But if this House votes that there is an emergency and the other House votes the other way, the vote in the other place has no effect and we are not stuck with some back and forth arrangement regarding conferences in an effort to get things sorted out while Canadians suffer from the cold.
I plead this case as strongly as I can, and I urge my hon. friends in the Progressive Conservative party to support me. Let me give them this word of commendation. I will
Energy Supplies Emergency Act commend them for having fought to get a reference to parliament into this bill, and here it is now before us. I will even take back some of the things I said a while ago and say that this is good. But having got it in the bill, let us not spoil it by giving a veto to the other place. My hon. friends of the Conservative party know how many Liberals there are in the other place and knowing how the other place is dominated by Liberals I am surprised that they would want to give them this extra power.
To my Liberal friends on the other side of the House I say, let them look at this proposal carefully and not be bound by any agreement that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) may have made with any spokesman for the Progressive Conservative party. Any agreement that we made for this motion requiring reference to parliament did not include veto power being given to the Senate.
Therefore, in support of this very strong plea that I urge upon this House, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas):
That Motion No. 4 be amended by deleting from the proposed subclause (9) of clause 11 of Bill C-236 the words "either House of Parliament" and by substituting therefor the words "the House of Commons".

Mr. Speaker, I was not a member of the committee to which this bill that we are reporting was referred. This is probably just as well because I must say that, while I found the revelations of what took place in the committee extremely interesting and would have liked to hear more about them, I am afraid the discussions of the internal details of the committee are obscuring an important point of principle which is raised by the amendment moved by my colleague. The important point of principle is one that I think we have to settle and that is whether the other place, a non-elected body, is the appropriate group to have the responsibility of determining whether an emergency of the type described in the measure exists in this country. I say emphatically that it is not; that a non-elected body is not an appropriate tribunal or authority for determing the existence of an emergency.
It would be absolutely unthinkable, after the government of this country, the executive, had determined that there was in fact a national emergency, and a matter which required extraordinary action and that decision had been upheld or approved by a motion of the elected members of this House of Commons, that this body which has no jurisdiction in this matter unless we choose to give it, the other place, should be given the responsibility of overriding a decision on this matter of the executive of the country and the decision of the House of Commons composed of elected members. It is no insult whatever to the other place. It is not quite correct to say that they are unrepresentative. They do represent certain interests. A number of directorships are held by members of the other place. I will not go into details, but it is well known that they represent a particular point of view. I, for one, other members of my party and, I hope, members of the House generally, do not accept the proposition that we should give to the other place the right to veto the will of the elected members of the House of Commons.
The principle embodied in motion No. 4-I am not talking of the amendment as a whole-is an advance. I was in the House when the War Measures Act was invoked by a decision of the executive. Their power to do that has been upheld by the courts on innumerable occasions. They are the authority which primarily determines the existence of the emergency. In that situation we, in this House, were asked to express our views as to whether an emergency existed. I was one of those who voted against the invocation of the War Measures Act, because I did not think that such an emergency existed as would justify the complete abolition of the constitution and the withdrawal of all the rights and liberties of the people. This is what was involved in any declaration that the War Measures Act had been invoked and was in force.
I submit that the elected branch of Parliament in which I am now speaking, the House of Commons, should have the right to pass judgment on whether the very strong powers-they need to be strong in an emergency-to be conferred by this statute are justified by the existence of a
January 9, 1974

real emergency. That, really, is what we are considering, and in that regard the provision before us represents a step forward. But, in giving the non-elected, unrepresentative members of the other place the power to intervene and say, "We say, from our limited point of view, that there is no emergency, and therefore the will of the people of Canada can be frustrated by our determination," we are taking not one step forward but two steps backward.
We are talking, simply, about a matter of principle. This has nothing to do with what went on in committee. I submit that the other place is not the appropriate body to determine this particular subject matter, important as it is to all the people of Canada. The Senate does not have the power under the constitution. Why should we give them that power by statute? It would be wrong of us to do so. I think we should be abandoning our responsibilities as elected representatives if we were to share our responsibility with a non-elective body and give them power to veto decisions which are the subject matter of this particular motion. We are not considering a statute. This is to be a resolution. I think it is perfectly appropriate for resolutions to be passed by the House of Commons, without reference to the other place.
For these reasons, I hope the House will determine to accept the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Let us pass the measure, and vest the ample power to check decisions in this elected House of Parliament; let us not resort to the other place which, for reasons I could elaborate on at length, is made up of the most inappropriate group possible to which this power should be given.

Mr. Speaker, may I emphasize some of the points raised by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) in support of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The amendment proposed by the minister, as printed on the order paper, is mostly the result of negotiation between the minister and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). As the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) pointed out in committee, they were busy working out last minute details. The amendment was never presented in written form in the committee. The committee agreed that it should be printed on the order paper for consideration at the report stage. This we are now doing and, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, we now see its weakness.
As the amendment proposed by the minister now stands, the Senate has the right to veto the decision of the elected members of this House. By giving that right to an appointed body we should be thwarting one of the basic principles of democracy. I am disappointed to note that members of the Conservative party so far have been supporting the amendment proposed by the minister.
If there is an emergency involving oil supplies, an emergency affecting thousands of Canadians, people in hospitals, children in schools and workers in industry, the responsibility for decision making should not rest with those who cannot speak for the people, but should rest with those who are elected in this chamber.
